claim: Most meetings need no physical co-location
originalWording: Most meetings need no physical co-location

sources.title: The Age of Spiritual Machines — Ray Kurzweil (1999)

sourceCaveat: The original book edition has not been independently checked. See the listed source on Sources for attribution limits.

strict.criterion: Most meetings require no physical co-location because immersive virtual-reality presence substitutes naturally for being in the same room.
strict.rationale: In The Age of Spiritual Machines, Kurzweil tied co-location-free 2019 meetings directly to high-resolution virtual-reality environments matching physical presence. Standard 2D video calls (Microsoft Teams had 13 million daily users in mid-2019, a small slice of the global workforce) did not deliver immersive VR presence, and even after the 2020 remote-work surge, organizations still treat in-person meetings as essential for many collaborations.
changedConditions: Retains the 2019 virtual-reality presence context and tests whether co-location became broadly unnecessary

evidence.title: Cisco announces acquisition of WebEx
evidence.note: WebEx had more than 2.2 million registered users; evidence of established distributed collaboration, not most employees working from home.

evidence.title: Microsoft Teams reaches 13 million daily active users
evidence.note: Primary institutional, research, or issuer source. Dates in the claim refer to the observation or product event, not the review date.

reference.criterion: Most ordinary information-sharing meetings can be conducted without co-location; the wording is about need, not actual venue share.
reference.rationale: Large-scale video and collaboration platforms already supported ordinary distributed meetings by 2019. The capability remains established. It would misread this claim to require proof that most meetings actually happened online.
